newsitem.title: USA: Prosecution case in Oklahoma bomb trial nears end.
newsitem.headline: Prosecution case in Oklahoma bomb trial nears end.

text.p: The prosecution case against accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh enters its final phase with the focus expected to turn to the controversial area of FBI analysis of crime scene evidence.

The closely-watched trial resumes on Monday after a three-day break for what sources close to the case said could be the last week of government evidence against McVeigh, 29, accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.
A string of FBI agents testified last week about the collection of evidence from the bomb site but they have so far said little about what the evidence showed.

Scott Robinson, a Denver lawyer and trial analyst, said he expected remaining prosecution witnesses to include Supervisory Special Agent Steven Burmeister from the Federal Bureau of Investigation's much-criticised laboratory in Washington D.C., and Linda Jones, a British explosives expert who has testified in Irish Republican Army trials in London.

Prosecutors may also call a handwriting expert to compare McVeigh's handwriting to that of the man who rented the Ryder truck allegedly used in the bombing, he said. The government says the man, who gave his name as Robert Kling, was McVeigh.
"They will call additional victims and survivors to testify about those who died in the blast ... after that, I anticipate the prosecution will rest, probably some time (this) week," Robinson said.
Over the past three weeks, 129 prosecution witnesses have given a wealth of circumstantial evidence against McVeigh, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of conspiracy and murder.

The prosecution has raced through its case that had been expected to take about seven weeks. The defence, which says McVeigh is innocent and has suggested the bombing could have been an international conspiracy, will then put on its case.

Prosecutors allege that McVeigh, a decorated Gulf War veteran, bombed the Murrah building to avenge the deaths of 80 Branch Davidian cult members in a clash with federal agents at Waco, Texas, on April 19, 1993, exactly two years earlier. McVeigh could face the death penalty if convicted. His friend, co-defendant Terry Nichols, will be tried separately later.

Denver's Rocky Mountain News reported on Sunday that prosecutors believe the main component of the Oklahoma City bomb was a version of ammonium nitrate specifically made for bombs, not fertiliser. It said explosives manufacturers used to funnel excess bomb-grade ammonium nitrate into the agricultural market to be sold as fertiliser, but had quietly changed the practice since the Oklahoma City blast.
Prosecutors will be treading on sensitive ground if, as expected, they introduce testimony about the analysis of bombing evidence at the FBI laboratory in Washington D.C.
Lab tests found traces of explosives on McVeigh's clothing but the defence was expected to argue that the clothes could have been contaminated by FBI mishandling.

A Department of Justice report released last month strongly criticised several FBI forensic scientists who worked on the Oklahoma City bombing case. It singled out FBI explosives unit examiner David Williams, who it said "repeatedly reached conclusions that incriminated the defendants without a scientific basis."
When the report came out, chief defence attorney Stephen Jones said he expected it to play some role in the trial.
Burmeister, who found traces of explosives on McVeigh's clothing, was not criticised in the report. The explosives expert was expected to confirm the FBI lab's findings.

Legal experts have praised the prosecution's methodical presentation of its case. Prosecutors have tried to keep jurors interested by alternating from dry discussions of evidence such as telephone records and the gripping stories of survivors who vividly recalled the human impact of the tragedy.
But the defence scored points last week when an FBI fingerprint expert said McVeigh's fingerprints were not found at several key locations.
